cards.front: {{c1::Homeostasis}} is keeping internal conditions within a stable range while the outside changes.
cards.quote: Homeostasis is keeping internal conditions within a stable range while the outside changes.

cards.front: Does homeostasis hold body temperature at one fixed number? Give the usual value and what it does through the day.
cards.back: No. It is usually near 37 °C, but it shifts a little through the day. Homeostasis keeps a range, not one number.
cards.quote: Body temperature is usually near 37 °C, but it shifts a little through the day.

cards.front: In a hot-room feedback simulation, the sensor is broken. What does the temperature graph do, and why?
cards.back: It stays away from the usual range. The change is never detected, so the control center never signals the sweat glands.
cards.why: The loop needs every part: change, sensor, control center, effector, response.
cards.quote: With the sensor broken, the change is never detected, so the control center never signals the sweat glands.
cards.section: Test the model in a simulation

cards.front: What is negative feedback?
cards.back: A loop in which the response opposes the change that started it, pushing the variable back toward its usual range.
cards.quote: a loop in which the response opposes the change that started it
cards.section: Name the parts of negative feedback

cards.front: In a feedback loop, a {{c1::sensor}} is a cell or organ that detects the change.
cards.quote: A sensor, a cell or organ that detects the change.
cards.section: Name the parts of negative feedback

cards.front: What does the control center do in a negative feedback loop?
cards.back: It compares the sensed value with the usual range and sends a signal.
cards.quote: A control center, which compares the sensed value with the usual range and sends a signal.
cards.section: Name the parts of negative feedback

cards.front: An {{c1::effector}} is a muscle, gland or cell that carries out the response in a feedback loop.
cards.quote: An effector, a muscle, gland or cell that carries out the response.
cards.section: Name the parts of negative feedback

cards.front: On a cold day, body temperature drifts down. Name two effector responses that push it back up.
cards.back: Muscles shiver, which releases heat, and skin blood vessels narrow, so less heat is lost.
cards.why: The same control center sends different signals for a change in the other direction.
cards.quote: Muscles shiver, which releases heat, and skin blood vessels narrow, so less heat is lost.
cards.section: Name the parts of negative feedback

cards.front: How does positive feedback differ from negative feedback?
cards.back: In positive feedback the response makes the change bigger until an event ends it, as in the contractions of childbirth.
cards.quote: In positive feedback, the response makes the change bigger until an event ends it, as in the contractions of childbirth.
cards.section: Name the parts of negative feedback

cards.front: How do the two sets of nerves reaching the heart change during exercise?
cards.back: One set speeds the heart and one slows it. Exercise turns up the first and turns down the second.
cards.quote: Two sets of nerves reach the heart: one speeds it and one slows it.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: A person stops exercising. What happens to the nerves that slow the heart, and when?
cards.back: The slowing nerve becomes active again, mostly in the first minutes, so heart rate falls.
cards.why: Exercise had turned it down; stopping reverses that.
cards.quote: When you stop, the slowing nerve becomes active again, mostly in the first minutes.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: During moderate exercise, why are carbon dioxide sensors not the main reason heart rate rises?
cards.back: Faster breathing keeps blood carbon dioxide fairly steady.
cards.quote: During moderate exercise, faster breathing keeps blood carbon dioxide fairly steady, so carbon dioxide sensors are not the main reason heart rate rises.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: Why is heart control during exercise more than one feedback loop?
cards.back: The brain also raises heart rate as exercise begins, partly through commands sent before any large change in the blood.
cards.quote: the brain raises heart rate as exercise begins, partly through commands sent before any large change in the blood
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: Each stoma in a leaf sits between two {{c1::guard cells}} that change shape to open or narrow it.
cards.quote: Stomata (one is a stoma) are the leaf's pores, and each sits between two guard cells that change shape to open or narrow it.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: On a dry afternoon, guard cells narrow a bean leaf's stomata. What result follows most directly?
cards.back: Water leaves the leaf more slowly.
cards.quote: On a dry afternoon, guard cells narrow a leaf's stomata, so water leaves more slowly.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: In one Arabidopsis preparation, warming opened pores, while dry air tends to narrow them. Can temperature alone predict what a whole plant's guard cells do on a hot afternoon?
cards.back: No. In a whole plant the response depends on several signals together: temperature, dry air and the water supply. "Hot means closed" is too simple.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that guard cells respond to several signals at once.
cards.quote: In a whole plant on a hot afternoon, what the guard cells do depends on several signals together, including temperature, dry air and the water supply.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: Why is hydrotropism, a root growing toward wetter soil, usually not called a complete feedback loop?
cards.back: It is slow compared with a heartbeat, and it changes the direction of growth rather than holding a number inside the plant within a range.
cards.quote: It is slow compared with a heartbeat, and it changes the direction of growth rather than holding a number inside the plant within a range.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: A cell membrane that lets some substances cross and holds others back is {{c1::selectively permeable}}.
cards.quote: Selectively permeable means it lets some substances cross and holds others back.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: What is passive transport across a membrane?
cards.back: Substances move from where they are more concentrated to where they are less, and the cell spends no energy.
cards.quote: In passive transport, substances move from where they are more concentrated to where they are less, and the cell spends no energy.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: A cell moves sodium out even though there is already more sodium outside than inside. Is this passive or active transport, and why?
cards.back: Active transport. The cell spends energy to move substances from less to more.
cards.quote: In active transport, the cell spends energy to move substances from less to more.
cards.section: What the four pictures leave out

cards.front: In a treadmill study of 52 adults, mean heart rate was 179 beats/min at peak, 145 at 1 minute after, and 75 at rest. About what fraction of the gap from peak to rest closed in the first minute?
cards.quote: The gap between peak (179) and the resting mean (75) is 104 beats/min, and the mean closed 34 of them in the first minute.
cards.section: Read the evidence: how fast does heart rate come back?

cards.front: In the same study, mean heart rate was 106 beats/min at 4 minutes and 102 at 5 minutes. What is the fall in that minute, and what does it say about the shape of the recovery graph?
cards.back: 106 − 102 = 4 beats/min, far less than the 34 in the first minute. The graph drops steeply early, then flattens.
cards.quote: A steep early drop that flattens out fits the published data.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the same study the 5-minute mean heart rate was 102 beats/min and the resting mean was 75. Was the group back to rest, and by how much did they differ?
cards.back: No. 102 − 75 = 27 beats/min above the resting mean.
cards.quote: These are means for 52 healthy adult volunteers on the first day of a treadmill study.
cards.section: Read the evidence: how fast does heart rate come back?

cards.front: The same volunteers had mean heart rates at 1 minute of 145, 144 and 145 beats/min on days 1, 7 and 30. What is the mean of the three values?
cards.quote: At each time, mean = sum of the three values ÷ 3.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a class investigation of heart rate after a short activity, name the independent variable, the dependent variable, and two things kept constant.
cards.back: Independent: time after the activity (0, 1, 2, 3 and 5 minutes). Dependent: heart rate in beats per minute. Constants: same activity for the same time, same sitting recovery position, same counting method, same room.
cards.quote: Independent variable: time after the activity (0, 1, 2, 3 and 5 minutes).
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a repeated-trial heart rate investigation, what should you do with a count you know was a mistake?
cards.back: Keep every value and mark the mistaken count, instead of deleting a result you did not expect.
cards.quote: Keep every value; mark a count you know was a mistake instead of deleting a result you did not expect.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: When counting pulse after exercise, what is the tradeoff between a full-minute count and a 15-second count multiplied by 4?
cards.back: A full-minute count averages that minute, so record when it started. Shorter counts show changes closer together but are only estimates of the rate.
cards.quote: Shorter counts, such as 15 seconds multiplied by 4, show changes closer together but are only estimates of the rate.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A student sees the group's mean heart rate still above rest at 5 minutes (102 versus 75 beats/min) and says the feedback loop failed. Evaluate the claim.
cards.back: The claim is not supported. After exercise the heart slows over several minutes toward its resting range, and the table is still falling (106 to 102), so recovery was in progress.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that opposing responses move a condition toward its range over time.
cards.quote: When you stop, they change, and it slows over several minutes toward its resting range.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking
